stem: A randomized trial compares a new antiplatelet drug with placebo in 800 adults followed for 2 years; 80% of eligible patients agreed to take part. Stroke occurs in 40 of 400 placebo patients and 24 of 400 drug patients.
oneliner: Antiplatelet vs placebo RCT, 800 adults (80% of eligible enrolled) + stroke 40/400 vs 24/400 → ARR?
ask: What is the absolute risk reduction?

whyNot.A: This is the **relative** risk reduction (0.04/0.10), not the absolute difference
whyNot.B: This is the **relative risk** (0.06/0.10 = 60%), a ratio rather than a difference
whyNot.D: 16/800 divides the difference by **both arms together**; each arm has 400
whyNot.E: Multiplies by the **enrolment fraction**, which does not enter the calculation

why: Placebo risk is 40/400 = 0.10 and drug risk is 24/400 = 0.06. **ARR = control risk − treated risk** = 0.10 − 0.06 = **0.04 = 4%**. Check: 16/400 = 0.04.

idea.rule: ARR = control event rate − treated event rate.
also: NNT = 1/ARR
RRR = ARR / control risk
Enrolment fraction is irrelevant to ARR
ARR is an absolute difference, so it carries the same units as risk

stem: A 5-year trial gives a statin or placebo to 500 adults with type 2 diabetes, 250 per arm. Myocardial infarction occurs in 30 placebo patients and 20 statin patients.
oneliner: Statin vs placebo in diabetes, 250 per arm + MI 30 vs 20 over 5 y → NNT?
ask: What is the number needed to treat to prevent one myocardial infarction?

whyNot.B: 1/RRR (1/0.333); the NNT uses the **absolute** reduction, not the relative one
whyNot.C: 1/**placebo risk** (1/0.12) ignores the benefit in the treated arm
whyNot.D: 1/**treated risk** (1/0.08) ignores the control arm
whyNot.E: This is the **patients per arm**, not a function of the risk difference

idea.rule: NNT = 1 / ARR.
also: NNH = 1 / absolute risk increase
A smaller ARR means a larger NNT
NNT is always rounded up to a whole patient in practice
Same relative reduction gives a smaller NNT when baseline risk is higher

stem: A vaccine trial enrols 600 nursing-home residents for one winter, 300 per arm. Pneumonia develops in 60 unvaccinated and 45 vaccinated residents.
oneliner: Nursing-home vaccine trial, 300 per arm + pneumonia 60 vs 45 → RRR?
ask: What is the relative risk reduction?

whyNot.A: This is the **absolute** risk reduction (0.20 − 0.15)
whyNot.B: This is the **relative risk** (0.15/0.20), not the reduction
whyNot.C: Divides by the **treated** risk (0.05/0.15) instead of the control risk
whyNot.D: This is the **NNT** (1/0.05), a count of patients rather than a percentage

why: Unvaccinated risk is 60/300 = 0.20 and vaccinated risk is 45/300 = 0.15, so ARR = 0.05. **RRR = ARR / control risk** = 0.05/0.20 = **25%**. Check: 1 − RR = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25.

idea.rule: RRR = ARR / control risk = 1 − RR.
also: RR = treated risk / control risk
Vaccine efficacy is the RRR
NNT = 1/ARR
RRR can look large even when the ARR is small

stem: A prospective cohort study follows 1,000 smokers and 2,000 nonsmokers for 10 years. Bladder cancer develops in 30 smokers and 20 nonsmokers.
oneliner: Cohort 1,000 smokers vs 2,000 nonsmokers + bladder cancer 30 vs 20 → RR?
ask: What is the relative risk of bladder cancer in smokers?

whyNot.A: 30/20 uses **raw case counts** and ignores the different group sizes
whyNot.C: This is the **inverted** ratio (nonsmoker over smoker risk)
whyNot.D: This is the risk **difference** (0.03 − 0.01), not a ratio
whyNot.E: 1/0.02 is a **number needed to harm**, a count of people rather than a ratio of risks

why: Smokers have a risk of 30/1000 = 0.03 and nonsmokers 20/2000 = 0.01. **RR = risk in exposed / risk in unexposed** = 0.03/0.01 = **3.0**. Check: (30 × 2000)/(1000 × 20) = 3.0.

idea.rule: RR = incidence in exposed / incidence in unexposed (cohort data).
also: RR > 1 means higher risk with exposure
RR = 1 means no association
Cohort studies give RR directly
Attributable risk = risk in exposed − risk in unexposed

stem: A case-control study compares 200 adults with pancreatic cancer and 200 controls for heavy alcohol use. Among cases, 80 report heavy use and 120 do not. Among controls, 40 report heavy use and 160 do not.
oneliner: Pancreatic cancer case-control, 200 cases/200 controls + heavy alcohol 80/120 vs 40/160 → OR?
ask: What is the odds ratio for heavy alcohol use?

whyNot.A: 80/40 compares **exposed cases to exposed controls** only
whyNot.B: This is bc/ad, the **inverted** odds ratio
whyNot.C: A **risk ratio** (0.67/0.43) treating the table as a cohort, which a case-control study cannot support
whyNot.E: This is the **proportion of cases exposed** (80/200), not an odds ratio

idea.rule: Case-control odds ratio = (a × d) / (b × c).
also: Case-control studies cannot give incidence or RR
OR approximates RR when the disease is rare
OR compares odds of exposure in cases and controls
OR > 1 means the exposure is associated with disease

stem: A case-control study of residence near power lines enrols 150 children with leukemia and 450 matched controls; the investigators chose 3 controls for each case. Of the 600 children, 120 live near power lines.
oneliner: Leukemia case-control, 150 cases + 450 controls (1:3 chosen), 120/600 near power lines → leukemia prevalence?
ask: What is the prevalence of leukemia in the population from these data?

whyNot.A: 150/600 only reflects the **1:3 ratio the investigators chose**
whyNot.B: 150/450 is the **case-to-control ratio**, set by the design
whyNot.C: 450/600 is the **control fraction**, also set by the design
whyNot.E: 120/600 is the **share of the sample exposed** to power lines, not the prevalence of leukemia

why: Investigators **fix the number of cases and controls**, so 150/600 = 25% only reflects the 1:3 sampling ratio; a 1:1 design would give 50%. **Case-control data cannot yield prevalence or incidence**, only an odds ratio.

idea.rule: Case-control data cannot give prevalence or incidence, because the investigator sets the case:control ratio.
also: Cohort studies give incidence and RR
Cross-sectional surveys give prevalence
Case-control studies give the odds ratio
Case-control suits rare diseases

stem: A new rapid strep test is compared with throat culture in 1,000 children with sore throat. Test positive and culture positive: 90; test positive and culture negative: 60; test negative and culture positive: 10; test negative and culture negative: 840.
oneliner: Rapid strep test vs culture in 1,000 children, TP 90, FP 60, FN 10, TN 840 → PPV?
ask: What is the positive predictive value of the rapid test?

whyNot.A: This is the **sensitivity** (90/100), which divides by the diseased
whyNot.C: This is the **specificity** (840/900), which divides by the non-diseased
whyNot.D: This is the **NPV** (840/850), which uses the negative-test column
whyNot.E: This is the **prevalence** (100/1000), not a test property

why: Positive tests total 90 + 60 = 150, of which 90 are true. **PPV = TP/(TP + FP)** = 90/150 = **60%**.

idea.rule: PPV = TP / (TP + FP): the chance of disease given a positive test.
also: NPV = TN / (TN + FN)
PPV rises with prevalence
Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN)
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)

stem: A D-dimer assay is compared with CT angiography in 200 emergency patients with suspected pulmonary embolism. Positive D-dimer with PE on CT: 40; positive D-dimer without PE: 20; negative D-dimer with PE: 10; negative D-dimer without PE: 130.
oneliner: D-dimer vs CT in 200 suspected PE, TP 40, FP 20, FN 10, TN 130 → NPV?
ask: What is the negative predictive value of the D-dimer?

whyNot.B: This is the **sensitivity** (40/50), which divides by the diseased
whyNot.C: This is the **specificity** (130/150), which divides by the non-diseased
whyNot.D: This is the **PPV** (40/60), which divides by all positive tests
whyNot.E: This is the **prevalence** (50/200), not a predictive value

why: Negative tests total 130 + 10 = 140, of which 130 are truly disease-free. **NPV = TN/(TN + FN)** = 130/140 = **93%**. Check: 1 − 10/140 = 0.929.

idea.rule: NPV = TN / (TN + FN): the chance of no disease given a negative test.
also: NPV falls as prevalence rises
A high NPV supports ruling out
PPV = TP / (TP + FP)
Predictive values depend on prevalence; sensitivity and specificity do not

stem: A 38-year-old woman has a positive result on a screening test. The test is used in 10,000 adults for a disease with 1% prevalence and has 90% sensitivity and 90% specificity.
oneliner: 38F + positive screen + prevalence 1% + sens 90%, spec 90% → PPV?
ask: Approximately what is the chance she has the disease?

whyNot.A: This is the **sensitivity**, not the probability of disease given a positive
whyNot.B: This is the **NPV** (8,910/8,920), not the PPV
whyNot.D: This is the **false-positive rate** (1 − specificity)
whyNot.E: This is the **prevalence**, the chance before testing

why: Of 10,000, 100 have disease (90 test positive, 10 negative) and 9,900 do not (990 test positive, 8,910 negative). **PPV = 90/(90 + 990)** = 90/1,080 = **8.3%**.

idea.rule: At low prevalence even a good test has a low PPV, because false positives outnumber true positives.
also: PPV rises with prevalence
NPV falls with prevalence
Screening low-risk groups yields many false positives
Build a 2 × 2 table from sensitivity, specificity and prevalence

stem: Mammography is compared with biopsy in 300 women with a breast lump. Among the 90 with cancer on biopsy, 72 have a positive mammogram and 18 a negative one. Among the 210 without cancer, 30 have a positive mammogram and 180 a negative one.
oneliner: Mammography vs biopsy in 300 women, cancer 72+/18−, no cancer 30+/180− → sensitivity?
ask: What is the sensitivity of mammography?

whyNot.A: This is the **specificity** (180/210), from the non-cancer group
whyNot.B: This is the **PPV** (72/102), which divides by all positives
whyNot.C: This is the **NPV** (180/198), which divides by all negatives
whyNot.D: 72/300 divides true positives by **everyone** tested

why: Of 90 women with cancer, 72 test positive. **Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN)** = 72/90 = **80%**. Check: 1 − 18/90 = 0.80.

idea.rule: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN): the share of diseased who test positive.
also: High sensitivity rules out disease (SnNout)
Sensitivity is unaffected by prevalence
False-negative rate = 1 − sensitivity
Screening tests favor high sensitivity

stem: A urine antigen test for Legionella is compared with culture in 1,000 adults with pneumonia. Among the 50 with Legionella on culture, 40 are antigen positive and 10 negative. Among the 950 without Legionella, 95 are antigen positive and 855 negative.
oneliner: Legionella urine antigen vs culture in 1,000 adults, culture+ 40/10, culture− 95/855 → specificity?
ask: What is the specificity of the urine antigen test?

whyNot.A: This is the **sensitivity** (40/50), from the Legionella group
whyNot.C: This is the **PPV** (40/135), which divides by all positives
whyNot.D: This is the **NPV** (855/865), which divides by all negatives
whyNot.E: This is the **false-positive rate** (95/950), the complement of specificity

why: Of 950 patients without Legionella, 855 test negative. **Specificity = TN/(TN + FP)** = 855/950 = **90%**. Check: 1 − 95/950 = 0.90.

idea.rule: Specificity = TN / (TN + FP): the share of non-diseased who test negative.
also: High specificity rules in disease (SpPin)
False-positive rate = 1 − specificity
Confirmatory tests favor high specificity
Specificity is unaffected by prevalence

stem: A 22-year-old woman has right lower quadrant pain and an ultrasound sign being evaluated for appendicitis. The sign has a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 90%.
oneliner: 22F + RLQ pain + ultrasound sign, sens 80%, spec 90% → LR+?
ask: What is the positive likelihood ratio of the sign?

whyNot.A: This is the **negative** LR, 0.2/0.9
whyNot.B: This is sensitivity/specificity (0.8/0.9), **not the LR formula**
whyNot.C: This is specificity/(1 − specificity), using the **wrong numerator**
whyNot.E: This is specificity/sensitivity, an **inverted** ratio

why: **LR+ = sensitivity/(1 − specificity)** = 0.80/0.10 = **8**. Check: true-positive rate 80% over false-positive rate 10%.

idea.rule: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity).
also: LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity
LR+ above 10 strongly rules in
LR− below 0.1 strongly rules out
LR = 1 leaves the probability unchanged

stem: A 59-year-old man has unilateral leg swelling and is assessed with a clinical decision rule for deep vein thrombosis. The rule has a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 80%.
oneliner: 59M + leg swelling + DVT rule, sens 95%, spec 80% → LR−?
ask: What is the negative likelihood ratio of the rule?

whyNot.B: This is the **positive** LR, 0.95/0.20
whyNot.C: This is the false-positive rate over specificity (0.2/0.8), using the **wrong numerator**
whyNot.D: This is **1 − sensitivity** alone, without dividing by specificity
whyNot.E: This is sensitivity/specificity, **not the LR formula**

why: **LR− = (1 − sensitivity)/specificity** = 0.05/0.80 = 0.0625, about **0.06**. A small LR− makes a negative result good for ruling out.

idea.rule: LR− = (1 − sensitivity) / specificity; a small LR− helps rule out.
also: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity)
LR− below 0.1 greatly lowers disease probability
LRs do not depend on prevalence
Post-test odds = pre-test odds × LR

stem: A 31-year-old man is screened for a viral infection with a two-test strategy in which he is called positive only if both tests are positive. Test A has 90% sensitivity and 80% specificity; test B has 80% sensitivity and 95% specificity. The tests err independently.
oneliner: 31M + two-test series strategy, A 90%/80%, B 80%/95%, both must be positive → net sens/spec?
ask: What are the net sensitivity and specificity of this strategy?

whyNot.A: This is the **parallel** strategy (either positive), not both
whyNot.B: Takes the **best of each**, which no combination guarantees
whyNot.C: Takes the **worst of each** value, not a calculation
whyNot.D: These are **averages**, but independent tests multiply

why: Both must be positive, so **net sensitivity = 0.90 × 0.80 = 72%**. A false positive needs both tests wrong: 0.20 × 0.05 = 0.01, so **net specificity = 99%**.

idea.rule: Series testing (both positive) lowers net sensitivity and raises net specificity.
also: Parallel testing (either positive) raises net sensitivity and lowers net specificity
Series confirms, as in an HIV antigen/antibody screen followed by a differentiation immunoassay
Parallel testing suits ruling out
Series net sensitivity = product of the sensitivities

stem: A one-day survey of 1,200 factory workers records smoking and current chronic cough. Of 300 smokers, 60 have cough; of 900 nonsmokers, 90 have cough.
oneliner: One-day survey of 1,200 workers + cough 60/300 smokers, 90/900 nonsmokers → overall prevalence?
ask: What is the overall prevalence of chronic cough in these workers?

whyNot.A: This is the prevalence in **smokers only** (60/300)
whyNot.B: This is the prevalence in **nonsmokers only** (90/900)
whyNot.D: This is the **prevalence ratio** (20%/10%), not a prevalence
whyNot.E: This is the **share of coughers who smoke** (60/150)

why: Total with cough is 60 + 90 = 150 of 1,200 workers. **Prevalence = existing cases / population at one time** = 150/1,200 = **12.5%**.

idea.rule: A cross-sectional survey measures prevalence at one point in time.
also: It cannot show temporality
It can compare prevalence between groups
It does not give incidence
Cohort studies give incidence

stem: In a study, 1,000 adults are screened for diabetes and then followed for 3 years. At baseline 100 already have diabetes. Over the 3 years, 45 of the remaining participants develop new diabetes.
oneliner: 1,000 screened + 100 diabetic at baseline + 45 new cases over 3 y → cumulative incidence?
ask: What is the 3-year cumulative incidence of diabetes?

whyNot.A: 45/1000 leaves the **prevalent cases in the denominator**
whyNot.B: This is the **baseline prevalence** (100/1000)
whyNot.D: This is **all cases** (145) over 1,000, mixing prevalent and new
whyNot.E: Counts the **prevalent cases in the numerator** (145/900)

why: People who already have diabetes cannot become new cases, so the population at risk is 1,000 − 100 = 900. **Incidence = new cases / population at risk** = 45/900 = **5%**.

idea.rule: Incidence = new cases / population at risk; existing cases leave the denominator.
also: Prevalence = all existing cases / total population
Prevalence ≈ incidence × mean duration
Incidence needs a follow-up period
Incidence is measured in cohort studies

stem: A town of 2,000 residents is surveyed for hepatitis C on January 1 and followed to December 31. On January 1, 80 residents have hepatitis C, and 40 more are diagnosed during the year. No one dies or moves away.
oneliner: Town of 2,000 + HCV 80 on Jan 1, 40 new during year → period prevalence?
ask: What is the period prevalence of hepatitis C for the year?

whyNot.A: This is the **point prevalence** on January 1 (80/2000)
whyNot.B: Counts **new cases only** (40/2000)
whyNot.C: This is the **incidence** (40/1920) among those at risk
whyNot.D: 120/1,920 uses the **population at risk** as denominator; prevalence divides by the whole population

why: Cases present at any time in the year are 80 + 40 = 120. **Period prevalence = (existing + new cases) / population** = 120/2,000 = **6%**.

idea.rule: Period prevalence = existing cases at the start plus new cases in the period, over the population.
also: Point prevalence counts one moment only
Incidence uses only new cases
Period prevalence is at least the point prevalence at the start
Prevalence includes old and new cases

stem: Towns X and Y have the same incidence of a chronic skin disease, 10 per 1,000 per year. Prevalence is 50 per 1,000 in town X and 20 per 1,000 in town Y.
oneliner: Skin disease, incidence 10/1,000/y in both towns, prevalence 50/1,000 in X (20/1,000 in Y) → mean duration in X?
ask: What is the average duration of the disease in town X?

whyNot.A: This is the duration in **town Y** (20/10)
whyNot.C: This is the **ratio of the two prevalences**, not a duration
whyNot.D: This is incidence/prevalence, **inverted**
whyNot.E: Reads the **prevalence count as years**

why: **Prevalence ≈ incidence × mean duration**, so duration = 0.050/0.010 per year = **5 years**. Check: 10/1,000 per year × 5 years = 50/1,000.

idea.rule: Prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration.
also: Longer duration raises prevalence at fixed incidence
Better treatment that prolongs survival raises prevalence
A fast cure lowers prevalence without changing incidence
Prevalence can rise while incidence is unchanged

stem: Fasting glucose is measured in 36 randomly chosen adults at a clinic. The sample mean is 100 mg/dL with a standard deviation of 18 mg/dL.
oneliner: 36 random adults + fasting glucose mean 100, SD 18 → 95% CI of the mean?
ask: What is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the mean?

whyNot.A: Uses the **SD** (about ±35) instead of the standard error
whyNot.B: Uses only **±1 SE**, which gives about a 68% interval
whyNot.C: Divides the SD by **n** (0.5) instead of by √n
whyNot.E: Uses **±3 SE**, a much wider interval (about 99.7%)

idea.rule: 95% CI of a mean = mean ± 1.96 × (SD / √n).
also: Larger n narrows the CI
SE shrinks with √n, not n
A 99% CI is wider than a 95% CI
SD describes spread of individuals; SE describes precision of the mean

stem: An observational study of diet and colon cancer reports five results: odds ratio 2.1 (95% CI 1.3 to 3.4); relative risk 1.4 (95% CI 0.9 to 2.2); risk difference 0.03 (95% CI −0.02 to 0.08); relative risk 0.8 (95% CI 0.6 to 1.05); and odds ratio 3.5 (95% CI 0.8 to 15.3).
oneliner: Diet and colon cancer study, five results with 95% CIs → which is significant?
ask: Which result is statistically significant at the 5% level?

whyNot.B: The interval **includes 1**, the null for a ratio
whyNot.C: The null for a difference is 0, and the interval **includes 0**
whyNot.D: The interval **just includes 1** at 1.05
whyNot.E: A large estimate but the interval **includes 1**

why: A ratio is significant only when its 95% CI **excludes 1**. Only the first interval (1.3 to 3.4) does; the others contain 1 (0.9–2.2, 0.6–1.05, 0.8–15.3), and the risk difference interval crosses its null of 0.

idea.rule: A ratio is significant if its 95% CI excludes 1; a difference is significant if its CI excludes 0.
also: CI crossing the null corresponds to p > 0.05
Wide CI means low precision
A CI shows the effect size, not just significance
A 95% CI excluding the null matches p < 0.05

stem: A 29-year-old man has a serum sodium of 143 mEq/L. In healthy adults of his age group, sodium is normally distributed with a mean of 140 mEq/L and a standard deviation of 3 mEq/L.
oneliner: 29M + Na 143 + healthy mean 140, SD 3, normal distribution → % of healthy above him?
ask: Approximately what percentage of healthy adults in his group have a higher sodium?

whyNot.A: This counts **both tails** beyond ±1 SD
whyNot.C: This is the area **between the mean and +1 SD**
whyNot.D: This is the area **within ±1 SD**
whyNot.E: This is the area beyond **+2 SD**, not +1

why: z = (143 − 140)/3 = 1. About 68% lies within 1 SD, so 32% lies outside and **half of that, 16%**, lies above. Check: 50% − 34% = 16%.

idea.rule: In a normal distribution about 16% lies above +1 SD and about 2.5% above +2 SD.
also: 68% within 1 SD
95% within 2 SD
99.7% within 3 SD
About 0.15% lies beyond +3 SD

stem: A 10-year-old girl takes an IQ test and scores 70. In her school district, scores are normally distributed with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15.
oneliner: 10F + IQ 70 + district mean 100, SD 15, normal → % scoring below her?
ask: Approximately what percentage of children in the district score lower?

whyNot.A: This counts **both tails** beyond ±2 SD
whyNot.B: This is the area below **−1 SD**, not −2
whyNot.C: This is the area below **−3 SD**
whyNot.E: This is the area **between the mean and −2 SD**

why: z = (70 − 100)/15 = −2. About 95% lies within 2 SD, so 5% lies outside and **half of that, 2.5%**, lies below. Check: 50% − 47.5% = 2.5%.

idea.rule: In a normal distribution about 2.5% lies below −2 SD and about 16% below −1 SD.
also: 68% within 1 SD
95% within 2 SD
99.7% within 3 SD
z-score = (value − mean) / SD

stem: Birth weights at a maternity hospital follow a normal distribution with a mean of 3400 g and an SD of 400 g. The unit labels any birth weight above 4600 g as macrosomia.
oneliner: Normal birth weights, mean 3400 g, SD 400 g, cutoff 4600 g → % above the cutoff?
ask: Using the 68-95-99.7 rule, about what percentage of newborns weigh more than 4600 g?

whyNot.B: **Both tails** together; the question asks only about weights above the cutoff
whyNot.C: The upper tail beyond **+2 SD**; 4600 g is 3 SD above the mean, not 2
whyNot.D: The upper tail beyond **+1 SD**, far too large for a cutoff 3 SD out
whyNot.E: The share **within** 3 SD of the mean, not the share above it

why: z = (4600 − 3400)/400 = **3**. About **99.7%** lie within 3 SD, so 0.3% lie outside in both tails and **half of that, 0.15%**, lies above +3 SD. Check: 50% − 49.85% = 0.15%.

idea.rule: Beyond +3 SD is about 0.15% (one tail); beyond ±3 SD is 0.3%.
also: Beyond +2 SD is about 2.5% (one tail)
Beyond +1 SD is about 16% (one tail)
Within ±1 SD is 68% and within ±2 SD is 95%

stem: A registry follows 1000 patients after diagnosis of a lymphoma. Year 1: 1000 alive at the start, 200 die. Year 2: 800 at the start, 80 die. Year 3: 720 at the start, 144 die. Year 4: 576 at the start, 72 die.
oneliner: Life table, 1000 patients, deaths 200/80/144/72 over 4 years → cumulative 4-year survival?
ask: What is the cumulative survival at the end of year 4?

whyNot.A: That is the **proportion who died** (1 − 0.504), not the proportion alive
whyNot.C: Drops **year 1** (0.90 × 0.80 × 0.875); the first interval must be included
whyNot.D: The **average** of the four interval survivals; survival is multiplied, not averaged
whyNot.E: Survival of the **last interval only**, not from diagnosis

idea.rule: Cumulative survival = product of the interval survival proportions.
also: Kaplan-Meier curve steps multiply in the same way
Interval survival = 1 − deaths/number at risk at the start of that interval
Cumulative survival can only stay the same or fall over time

stem: A 58-year-old man has just reached the 3-year mark after a diagnosis of dilated cardiomyopathy and asks about the coming year. A registry of 500 patients shows: Year 1: 500 alive at the start, 50 die. Year 2: 450 at the start, 90 die. Year 3: 360 at the start, 36 die. Year 4: 324 at the start, 81 die.
oneliner: 58M + alive at 3 years + life table (year 4: 324 at start, 81 die) → chance of surviving year 4?
ask: What is the probability that he survives year 4?

whyNot.A: The **chance of dying** in year 4 (81/324), not of surviving it
whyNot.B: **Cumulative** 4-year survival from diagnosis; he is already alive at 3 years
whyNot.C: Proportion **alive at 3 years from the start** (324/500), not year-4 survival
whyNot.D: Multiplies years 3 and 4 (0.90 × 0.75); **year 3 is already behind him**

why: He is already alive at the start of year 4, so only that interval counts. Survival = (324 − 81)/324 = 243/324 = **0.75**. Check: 1 − 81/324 = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75.

idea.rule: Survival through one interval, given alive at its start, is that interval's own survival proportion.
also: Earlier intervals do not enter a conditional question
Interval survival = 1 − deaths/number at risk at the start
The cumulative figure is for a patient at diagnosis, not later

stem: A 61-year-old woman has been alive for 2 years since a diagnosis of dilated cardiomyopathy and asks about her outlook to the end of year 4. A registry of 500 patients shows: Year 1: 500 alive at the start, 50 die. Year 2: 450 at the start, 90 die. Year 3: 360 at the start, 36 die. Year 4: 324 at the start, 81 die.
oneliner: 61F + alive at 2 years + life table (500/450/360/324 at start) → chance of being alive at 4 years?
ask: What is the probability that she is alive at the end of year 4?

whyNot.A: **Cumulative** survival from diagnosis (0.90 × 0.80 × 0.90 × 0.75); she is already alive at 2 years
whyNot.B: Multiplies years 1, 2 and 4 (0.72 × 0.75); **drops year 3** and includes the intervals she has already survived
whyNot.D: Years 1 and 2 only (0.90 × 0.80); those are **behind her**, years 3 and 4 are ahead
whyNot.E: **Year 4 only**; she must also survive year 3

why: Only years 3 and 4 remain. Year 3 survival is 324/360 = 0.90 and year 4 survival is 243/324 = 0.75, so 0.90 × 0.75 = **0.675**. Check: alive at 4 years / alive at 2 years = 243/360 = 0.675.

idea.rule: Conditional survival = product of only the interval survivals still ahead.
also: Equals (cumulative survival at the later time) ÷ (cumulative survival at the earlier time)
Cumulative survival from diagnosis here is 0.486
A patient who has survived longer has a better outlook than at diagnosis

stem: A trial is planned with a two-sided alpha of 0.05 and 90% power to detect a 5 mmHg difference in blood pressure. In truth, the drug has no effect at all.
oneliner: Trial alpha 0.05, power 90%, drug truly ineffective → chance of a significant result?
ask: What is the probability that this trial reports a statistically significant difference?

whyNot.A: A true null can still give a significant result by chance; the chance is **alpha**, not zero
whyNot.C: That is **beta** (1 − power), the miss rate when a true difference exists
whyNot.D: That is **power**, which applies only when a true difference exists
whyNot.E: That is **1 − alpha**, the chance of a non-significant result under the null

why: When the null hypothesis is true, a significant result is a false positive (**type I error**), and its probability is set by **alpha = 5%**. Beta = 1 − 0.90 = 10% and power apply only if a real 5 mmHg difference exists.

idea.rule: Under the null, P(significant) = alpha; under a true effect, P(significant) = power = 1 − beta.
also: Type I error = rejecting a true null
Type II error = failing to reject a false null
Lowering alpha cuts false positives but lowers power at fixed sample size

stem: In a cohort of 2000 adults, 1000 took a new antibiotic and 1000 did not. Within a month, severe rash developed in 30 of the 1000 exposed and in 10 of the 1000 unexposed.
oneliner: Rash 30/1000 on antibiotic vs 10/1000 without → number needed to harm?
ask: What is the number needed to harm?

whyNot.A: 1/0.67 uses the **attributable risk percent** (0.02/0.03) instead of the risk difference
whyNot.B: 1/0.04 **adds** the two risks (0.03 + 0.01) instead of subtracting them
whyNot.C: 1/0.03 uses the **exposed risk** alone instead of the risk difference
whyNot.E: 1/0.01 uses the **unexposed risk** alone instead of the risk difference

idea.rule: NNH = 1 / attributable risk (risk difference).
also: NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction
A larger risk difference gives a smaller number needed
Relative risk alone does not give NNH

stem: In a prospective cohort study, coffee drinkers have twice the risk of myocardial infarction of non-drinkers (crude RR 2.0). Coffee drinkers also smoke more. When the analysis is split by smoking status, the RR is 1.0 in smokers and 1.0 in nonsmokers.
oneliner: Coffee and MI: crude RR 2.0, smokers RR 1.0, nonsmokers RR 1.0, coffee drinkers smoke more → role of smoking?
ask: Which best describes the role of smoking in this association?

whyNot.A: Effect modification needs **different** RRs in the strata; here both are 1.0
whyNot.B: Nothing in the stem suggests a **biased choice of participants**; the clue is the stratified RRs
whyNot.C: Exposure was recorded **before the outcome** in a prospective cohort, so recall cannot differ by outcome
whyNot.E: Within each smoking group the RR is **1.0**, so no coffee effect remains

why: The stratum-specific RRs (**1.0 and 1.0**) are equal to each other but differ from the crude RR of 2.0. Smoking is linked to both coffee drinking and MI, so it **confounds** the crude association, and no true coffee effect remains.

idea.rule: Equal stratum RRs that differ from the crude RR mean confounding; different stratum RRs mean effect modification.
also: Confounding is removed by stratification, matching or regression adjustment
Effect modification is reported per stratum, not adjusted away
A confounder must be linked to both exposure and outcome and not lie on the causal path

stem: A prospective cohort study of oral contraceptive use and venous thrombosis is analyzed overall and then split by factor V Leiden status. The crude RR is 3.0. The RR is 8.0 in carriers of the mutation and 2.0 in non-carriers, and the two stratum confidence intervals do not overlap.
oneliner: OCP and venous thrombosis: crude RR 3.0, carriers RR 8.0, non-carriers RR 2.0 → role of factor V Leiden?
ask: Which best describes the role of factor V Leiden?

options.A: Effect modification by factor V Leiden

whyNot.B: Confounding gives **equal** stratum RRs that differ from the crude; here the strata differ (8.0 vs 2.0)
whyNot.C: Both strata have an RR **well above 1.0**
whyNot.D: Exposure was recorded **before the outcome** in a prospective cohort; the clue is the stratum RRs
whyNot.E: The stratum **confidence intervals do not overlap**, so chance alone does not explain 8.0 vs 2.0

answer: Effect modification by factor V Leiden
why: The stratum-specific RRs **differ from each other (8.0 vs 2.0)**, so the strength of the oral contraceptive effect depends on factor V Leiden status. The crude 3.0 hides this, so the strata are **reported separately** rather than adjusted into one number.

idea.rule: Different stratum-specific RRs = effect modification (interaction); report each stratum.
also: Genetic susceptibility that amplifies an exposure effect
Drug effect that differs by age group or sex
Smoking and asbestos multiply lung cancer risk together

stem: In a study of 400 adults, the Pearson correlation between body mass index and systolic blood pressure is r = 0.7.
oneliner: BMI vs systolic BP in 400 adults, r = 0.7 → variance in BP explained by BMI?
ask: What proportion of the variance in systolic blood pressure is explained by BMI?

whyNot.A: That is **1 − r**; r must be squared, not subtracted
whyNot.C: That is **1 − r²**, the variance left **unexplained**
whyNot.D: That is **r** itself, not the variance explained
whyNot.E: That is the **square root** of r; the variance explained is r squared

why: The coefficient of determination is **r²** = 0.7 × 0.7 = **0.49**. So 49% of the variance in blood pressure is explained by BMI, and 51% is not.

idea.rule: Variance explained = r² (coefficient of determination).
also: r = 0.5 explains 25% of variance
r ranges from −1 to +1; r² is always 0 to 1
Correlation does not prove causation
In simple linear regression, r² equals the squared correlation coefficient
